title: firstmate reviews its own recent work across all its projects on a schedule and proposes improvements for the captain to approve item by item
public_title: Add a periodic retrospective with per-item approval
acceptance: Why. firstmate has no habit of looking back. Pull requests go from task to merge through specs, worker rounds, reviews, CI runs and captain cards, in this repository and in the other repositories firstmate drives (external projects: the entries in config.yaml whose repo is not '.', each with its own private state, reviewers and CI). Nobody later asks what went wrong, what a simpler answer would have been, or what has gone stale. On 2026-10-09 one pull request in this repository spent seven review rounds and four spec versions chasing rare Git configuration cases before the captain narrowed it; four worker rounds on three tasks stopped on the same 'earlier work exists' confusion; and the engine checkout had to be fast-forwarded by hand after every merge. The only retrospective so far, state/reports/2026-10-08-codex-firstmate-retro.md, was a one-off written by hand. The captain asked for a recurring self-review of all projects that lists improvements as work items for approval.

How. A retrospective (retro for short) runs in three steps. First, a script computes facts about every pull request merged since the last retro in every configured project, with no model involved. Second, one reviewer round per project reads that project's facts, plus one more round reads the anonymised facts of all projects together; each round runs in the read-only sandbox reviews use. Third, firstmate shows the result as one summary card on the local board where the captain approves, parks or drops each proposed work item. Approved items then become normal tasks through the usual spec check and dispatch card, in the project they belong to. A retro never changes, deletes or dispatches anything by itself.

Privacy rule. Text that names an external project, its repository, owner, company, reviewers or private paths (identifying text) never enters this repository's committed files: specs under design/tasks/, tests, fixtures, design/design.md, design/diagrams/, skills, README, commit messages and pull request bodies. External metrics, reviewer prompts, reports, items, proposal drafts and task links live only in that project's private state directory (FM_STATE_DIR as set by fm_storage_init in bin/fm-config.sh). Work items for an external project become tasks in that project's private tasks directory (FM_TASKS_DIR). Items meant for firstmate itself carry no identifying text. Two narrow local exceptions exist, both in the self state directory, which is never committed: (1) the summary card's own records (state/pending/<id>.json, state/decisions/<id>.json, state/runtime/archived-pending/<id>.json if the card is archived, and the board's answer record for that card) may hold external item text so the captain can read it; (2) state/retro/<run-id>/private/labels.json holds the mapping from opaque label to project name and is read only by bin/lib/fm_retro.py. Nothing else outside a project's private state may hold its identifying text: not other self state/retro files, not any round's prompt except that project's own round, not the card's diagram, not self task proposals. All test fixtures use made-up project names.

Identifying text check. Before writing anything outside a project's private state, other than the two exceptions in 'Privacy rule', bin/lib/fm_retro.py checks the text against every external project's identifying tokens: the names that bin/lib/fm_private_names.py already derives from config.yaml (names(), and digest() for comparing against tests/fixtures/private-name-digests.txt), plus each external project's configured reviewer names and its FM_STATE_DIR and FM_TASKS_DIR paths. A field that matches is not written. A sentinel test registers a made-up external project, feeds its sentinel name through every stage (metrics, a project round's generic statements, the cross-project round, the card, the card's archival, an approved external item's claim and proposal, a firstmate item's proposal), and shows the sentinel appears in that project's private state and in the two allowed local exceptions, and nowhere else: not in any other self state/retro file, the cross-project prompt, the card diagram, design/, tests/ or any self proposal. tests/private-names.test.sh and tests/external-private-text.test.sh keep passing.

Opaque labels. Each external project gets a durable opaque label 'P-' followed by the first 8 hexadecimal digits of SHA-256 over a random salt (created once in state/retro/salt) and the project name, so the label does not change when config.yaml is reordered. The self project is 'self' and cross-project items are 'firstmate'. At the start of each run, fm_retro.py resolves every configured project's label once and writes the mapping to the run's private/labels.json; that run uses only this mapping. A project that is later removed from config.yaml keeps its label in old runs: its items on an open card still show and can be answered, but claim refuses them with reason 'project removed', and its parked items are no longer carried. Tests cover reordering and removing a project while its card and a claim are in flight.

Self-project runs. Every retro entry point (bin/fm-retro.sh, bin/fm-review.sh --retro, the board's POST /retro, and the autopilot's due check) runs from the engine checkout with the self project's context, and refuses with exit 64 (HTTP 400 on the board) when called with FM_EXTERNAL=1. It reads each external project by calling fm_storage_init for that project's name explicitly, never by inheriting the caller's environment.

Retro record. The durable record is state/retro/index.json in the self state, schema 1: {schema:1, baseline_at, last_completed: null or {run_id, window_end, completed_at}, open_run: null or run_id}. It holds no project names. Times are ISO 8601 UTC strings. Every read-modify-write of index.json and of a run's state.json happens while holding an exclusive lock on state/retro/index.lock (fcntl.flock, taken by bin/lib/fm_retro.py, which is the only writer; the board and the autopilot call it instead of writing the files themselves). baseline_at is written once, under that lock, the first time any entry point finds no index. Writes are atomic (temporary file in the same directory, then rename). window_end only moves forward; a write that would move it back is refused. Tests cover two concurrent first initializations (one baseline survives) and a completion racing a new run.

When a retro is due. One counter covers all projects, so the captain gets one retro and one card, and patterns shared by several projects are seen together; per-project counters would give several small cards and starve projects with few merges of the cross-project view. Let start be last_completed.window_end, or baseline_at when no retro has completed, and clock_start be last_completed.completed_at, or baseline_at. A retro is due when (a) at least 7 days (604800 seconds) have passed since clock_start, or (b) at least 10 pull requests, counted across every configured project, have a merged event in that project's state/events.jsonl newer than start; and (c) open_run is null. A late answer therefore moves the 7-day clock to the answer time, while the merge count still starts at the previous window end. Tests cover exactly 7 days and 6 days 23 hours, exactly 10 and 9 merges split across two projects, the first run after the baseline, a late answer, and a restart.

Autopilot wake. On each poll, the self project's autopilot (bin/lib/fm_autopilot.py) asks fm_retro.py for the due state and, when due, calls its existing queue() method (bin/lib/fm_autopilot.py:185) with the stable identity 'retro-due-' + (last_completed.run_id, or 'initial'), task None, and the line 'retro due'. queue() records each identity once, so repeated polls and restarts give one wake per window; a failed run keeps the identity, so it does not wake again; the identity changes only when a run completes. External projects' autopilots do not check. The autopilot never starts a retro, runs a model or creates a card, and its saved state gains no new required key. Tests cover repeated ticks, a restart before completion, a failed run, the next window, and an external project's autopilot.

Captain trigger. The board gains one button, 'Run retrospective', in the header area, labelled in the three board languages. It sends POST /retro with an empty JSON body; a body naming a project is refused with 400. The board accepts it only with the signed-in write access that answering a card needs (the existing writeRefusal check). It calls 'python3 bin/lib/fm_retro.py request', which under the index lock refuses (exit 75, board 409 code retroBusy) when open_run is set or a request is already waiting, and otherwise creates state/retro/requests/<request-id>.json by exclusive creation with {schema:1, requested_at, source:'board'}. The board then pushes a wake through a new pushRetroWake function next to the existing pushWake (board/server.ts, about line 1870), appending {id:'retro-request-<request-id>', reason:'retro_requested', woken} to the self project's state/session/wake.jsonl and ringing the bells the same way. The board never runs a retro. Tests cover the signed-out refusal, a project in the body, the 409 while a run is open, and two simultaneous requests (one accepted, one 409).

Run states and ownership. bin/fm-retro.sh subcommands: status, run, card, record, claim, link. A run id is the UTC start time YYYYMMDDTHHMMSSZ plus '-' and 6 random hexadecimal digits; its self directory state/retro/<run-id>/ is created by exclusive mkdir, and a collision draws a new suffix. state.json holds one of: running, reviewed, awaiting-answer, completed, failed, with timestamps and a failure reason. run first takes a non-blocking exclusive flock on state/retro/run.lock and keeps it until it exits; if the lock is held, it refuses ('a retro is running'). Then, under the index lock: if open_run names a run in state running (its owner must have died, because run.lock was free), that run becomes failed with reason 'interrupted' and open_run is cleared; if open_run names a run in reviewed or awaiting-answer, run refuses. It then creates the new run directory, writes state running, and sets open_run. A run that fails clears open_run. A waiting board request is moved into the new run's directory. firstmate starts run under bin/lib/fm-lifeline.sh. Tests cover a held lock, a dead owner before and after open_run was written, two starts within one second, and a retry after failure.

Window. A retro covers, for every configured project, the pull requests whose merged event (type 'merged' in that project's state/events.jsonl) is newer than start and not newer than the run's start time, which becomes the run's window_end.

Per-project records. For each project that gets a round, the run keeps that project's files in that project's own private state: for the self project under state/retro/<run-id>/projects/self/, and for an external project under <its FM_STATE_DIR>/retro/<run-id>/. Each holds metrics.json, metrics.md, a copy of the round's prompt (prompt.txt), report.md, items.json and that project's proposal manifests. The self run directory holds state.json, card.json, card-items.json, answers.json, the self proposal manifests, the cross-project round's files and private/labels.json; apart from the two exceptions in 'Privacy rule' and the self project's own files, nothing in it holds identifying text.

Metrics rules. bin/lib/fm_retro.py computes per pull request, from that project's local records only (its state/events.jsonl, its evidence store as opened by Store in bin/lib/fm_evidence.py with external set for external projects, its pins, its decisions and its run identities): task, the task id on the merged event or null for a pull request merged from an untracked merge card; worker_attempts, the number of 'dispatched' events for the task whose actor starts with 'worker-'; worker_rounds, the number of distinct 'round' values in those actors' state/runs/<actor>/identity.json; dispatch_to_merge_seconds, merged event time minus the first such dispatched event time; spec_versions, the number of distinct SHA-256 values of snapshots.spec.text across the task's pin files, with pins ordered by the integer in their file name (so 10 sorts after 2); scope_first and scope_last, the scope lists in the lowest and highest pin, and scope_added and scope_removed, the paths added and removed between them; review_rejections, the number of evidence records of kind 'verdict' whose verdict field is 'REJECT'; external_findings, for an external project, the number of distinct finding ids across the task's 'external-verdict' evidence records, which bin/lib/fm_external.py retains (about line 189) with the repository reviewers' findings, and null for the self project; stops, counts by category, where the category is the first ASK-<WORDS> marker in an 'ask' evidence record, or 'WORKER_BLOCKED' when only that marker is present; cards, [{id, purpose, chosen}] of the task's answered decisions.

Standing items. Each verdict record's text is parsed with the existing criteria(text, task) reader in bin/lib/fm_evidence.py (about line 47). An item's status token is read from its body after trimming leading and trailing whitespace and then leading '*' and '_' characters: it is the longest leading run of letters and hyphens, lowercased. 'open' counts as open, 'done' and 'ok' as closed; any other token is unreadable. For each item number, open_rounds is the number of verdicts in which it is open. When any verdict of the task has no readable list or an unreadable token, standing is null. Fixtures include labelled items such as '4. **open — ...**', '7. gap NEW-GROUND: ...' (unreadable) and '2. done: ...'.

CI rules. For each pull request, fm_retro.py lists the GitHub Actions workflow runs of that project's repository for the pull request's head branch (GET actions/runs?branch=<branch>, 100 per page, at most 10 pages) through fm_github in bin/fm-config.sh, using GET requests only, in that project's context. It keeps runs whose pull_requests list contains the pull request number, which also covers rewritten heads. Runs are ordered by created_at. For each kept run with run_attempt n, it reads attempts 1 to n (GET actions/runs/<id>/attempts/<k>). Each failed attempt (conclusion failure, cancelled or timed_out) is classified, comparing only runs of the same workflow_id: 'infrastructure' when cancelled or timed_out; else 'flaky' when a later attempt of the same run concluded success; else 'real' when a later run of the same workflow on a different head_sha concluded success and no attempt on the failed head_sha did; else 'unknown'. reruns is the sum over distinct run ids of (run_attempt - 1). An attempt that cannot be read counts as unknown. When the 10-page cap is reached, or the repository has no Actions history, or GitHub cannot be reached, ci is null and the reason ('truncated', 'no actions history', 'unreachable') is recorded. Tests cover an unrelated green workflow, a rewritten head, repeated attempts, a cancellation followed by a successful rerun, an unreadable attempt, the page cap, and unreachable history.

Metrics output. Each project's metrics.json is {schema:1, run_id, project_label, window:{start, end}, generated_at, prs:[row], totals}. Every row has all of these fields: pr (integer), task (string or null), merged_at (string), worker_attempts, worker_rounds, dispatch_to_merge_seconds, spec_versions, review_rejections, external_findings (integers or null), scope_first, scope_last, scope_added, scope_removed (lists of strings or null), standing (list of {n, open_rounds} or null), stops (object of category to integer, or null), cards (list or null), ci ({red:{real, flaky, infrastructure, unknown}, reruns} or null), ci_reason (string or null), unknown (list of field names that are null). For a taskless row every task-derived field is null and listed in unknown. totals is {field: {sum, known_rows}} for each integer field, stops: {category: {sum, known_rows}}, and ci: {real, flaky, infrastructure, unknown, reruns}, each {sum, known_rows}; so missing data stays visible instead of counting as zero, following bin/lib/fm_round_metrics.py, which reports unavailable data as unavailable. metrics.md shows the same data as a table. A fixture test checks every field of a task row, a taskless row and the totals.

Project rounds. bin/fm-review.sh gains a --retro <run-id> mode with --project <name>. Like --spec-preflight (bin/fm-review.sh about line 97), it routes early to its own launcher, a new bin/lib/fm-retro-review.sh, before any pull request, pin or ordinary verdict logic. It runs one reviewer round per eligible project (one that has pull requests in the window, approved items awaiting follow-up, or parked items), with the reviewer sandbox policy for that project (read-only; no state directory is readable, neither the self state nor any project's private state), on a fresh checkout of the engine's current base commit, under the same lifeline, run directory handling and authenticated final-answer selection that reviews use, emitting the usual lifecycle events with mode 'retro'. An external project's round keeps its run directory and output in that project's private state, as its existing reviews do. The external repository's code is not checked out: the questions are about how firstmate worked on it.

Cross-project round. After all project rounds, one more round (--retro <run-id> --retro-cross, self context) runs on the engine checkout. It runs whenever any project round ran or any 'firstmate' item is approved and awaiting follow-up or parked. Its prompt holds only: an anonymous projection of each project's metrics; the generic statements that passed the identifying text check; the approved 'firstmate' items awaiting follow-up, each with its self manifest's task link, the anonymous projection of its baseline metrics and the linked task's metrics row if merged; and the parked 'firstmate' items under the same caps as a project round. The projection keeps, per row: a row number instead of the pull request number, merged_at, worker_attempts, worker_rounds, dispatch_to_merge_seconds, spec_versions, review_rejections, external_findings, the lengths of scope_first and scope_last and the counts of scope_added and scope_removed instead of the paths, standing, stops with each category checked (a refused category becomes 'REDACTED'), cards as counts by purpose and chosen option instead of ids, ci and ci_reason; plus the project's opaque label. A refused generic statement is dropped and recorded as {label, index, refused:true}. No projection field can carry identifying text, so a refusal never fails the run. Its output is checked again before it is written. Tests show that identifying scope paths, decision ids and task ids never reach the projection. Tests cover an approved and a parked 'firstmate' item with no merges in the window.

Retro vendor and model. Every retro round's vendor and model come from a new config.yaml section, retro:, set to vendor claude and model claude-opus-5-5, so the reviewer and worker settings do not change. The existing lookups (fm_cfg_in and fm_model_for in bin/fm-config.sh) read it with role 'retro'. When the section or either key is missing, run refuses with exit 65 and a message naming the missing key, instead of using another vendor. The sandbox policy uses the 'reviewer' role in bin/lib/fm_registry.py, which stays unchanged.

Reviewer inputs. No state directory is readable in the sandbox, so each round's inputs travel in its prompt, through the same standard-input prompt stream that every round already uses (bin/fm-sandbox.sh about line 125), not as extra files. A project round's prompt holds: its project's metrics.json; for each of its pull requests, the task title and acceptance lines, the text of its REJECT verdicts, its worker stop records and, for an external project, its retained repository-reviewer findings; its project's approved items awaiting follow-up with their links and baseline metrics; and its parked items. A round never receives another project's text. Each optional text is cut to at most 2,000 characters at a character boundary and marked '[cut: kept N of M characters]', and carries a stable reference (pull request number, task id, evidence file name). The mandatory part is: metrics.json, at most 50 follow-up items, at most 50 full parked items, at most 500 older parked item ids (beyond that only their count), and one drop summary line. When the mandatory part alone exceeds 200,000 characters, that round is not started and the run fails with reason 'inputs too large'. Otherwise optional texts are added oldest pull request last until the prompt would exceed 200,000 characters; the drop summary line states how many were left out and lists at most 100 references. Tests cover project separation, a metrics overflow, a parked-id overflow, a follow-up overflow, and that the prompt carries the inputs while the state directories stay unreadable.

Five questions. A project round runs for every project that has pull requests in the window, or approved items awaiting follow-up, or parked items. It answers, with evidence for every finding (a metric field, a pull request, an evidence reference, or a file:line in the engine): (a) what went wrong in the process from task to merge for that project; (b) from first principles, what simpler or more fundamental solution would have avoided it, looking first for something to delete or simplify; (c) which firstmate tests, scripts or skills are obsolete or replaced, with evidence such as no remaining caller, coverage duplicated by another named test, or replaced by a named newer part; (d) after re-reading firstmate's architecture in design/design.md and its diagrams, which parts are wrong, redundant or could be simpler; (e) for each of that project's approved items, whether the related metrics improved. The cross-project round answers (a), (b) and (d) for patterns seen in more than one project, and (e) for approved 'firstmate' items. Tests cover a project with an approved, unmerged task and zero merges in the window, and an approved 'firstmate' item.

Follow-up of approved items. Before firstmate writes a task proposal for an approved item, it runs bin/fm-retro.sh claim --run <run-id> --item <label>/<item-id>. Under the index lock this creates, by exclusive creation, a manifest in the item's own project: for an external item <its FM_STATE_DIR>/retro/<run-id>/proposals/<item-id>.json, holding status 'proposing', the private draft path and later the task id; and in the self run directory proposals/<label>-<item-id>.json holding only {status} ('proposing', 'linked' or 'refused'), with no path or task id for external items. A 'firstmate' item's self manifest also holds its draft path under design/tasks/ and task id, which carry no identifying text. After the task exists, link --run --item --task updates both manifests to 'linked'. For an external item the private manifest is authoritative and is always written first, both on claim and on link; the self manifest follows. Reconciliation, under the lock, repairs the self manifest from the private one when they disagree or the self one is missing, and removes a self manifest whose private manifest does not exist (the claim never happened). When the project has been removed and its private manifest cannot be opened, the self manifest becomes 'refused' with reason 'project removed'. After a restart, firstmate resumes every 'proposing' item from its recorded draft and never claims an item twice. The baseline for question (e) is the metrics.json of the run that proposed the item; the next retro gives each approved item with its link and the linked task's metrics row if its pull request has merged, otherwise the label 'not yet measurable'. Tests cover a crash between the two claim writes, between the two link writes, after link, project removal during that recovery (always exactly one proposal), an item whose task has not merged, and that no external path or task id reaches a self manifest, the cross-project prompt or a committed file.

Proposals only. Retro rounds propose; they never delete, edit, commit or dispatch. A cleanup finding names the files and the evidence; deleting them is a later normal task the captain approves. A finding that needs a captain decision about direction says so and asks the question instead of proposing a change.

Removal first. The retro prefers taking things away over adding new protocol (captain, 2026-10-09). Every item states what it deletes or simplifies: code, tests, rules, steps or files, named concretely. An item that adds protocol surface (a new rule, command, file format, state, field, gate, card type or check) must also say why a simpler removal cannot solve the problem; an adding item without that justification makes the round's report invalid, like any other format error. Within each round's report and on the summary card, items that only remove or simplify come first, then items that remove more than they add, then items that add surface, each group ordered by item id.

Report format. Each round's final answer contains a readable report and exactly one fenced code block whose info string is retro-items, holding JSON {schema:1, items:[...], generic:[...]}. items has 0 to 20 entries per round, each: id (string R1, R2, ..., unique within the round), kind (process, simplify, cleanup, architecture or followup), carried_from (null, or '<run-id>/<project-label>/<id>' of a parked item it repeats), effect (one of 'removes', 'net-removal', 'adds'), removes (1 to 20 strings naming what it deletes or simplifies; may be empty only when effect is 'adds'), and for both en and zh-TW an object with title, why and how (strings), evidence (1 to 10 strings), scope (0 to 20 path strings) and, when effect is 'adds', why_not_removal (a string saying why a simpler removal cannot solve it). generic (project rounds only) has 0 to 10 strings, each a pattern stated without identifying text, for the cross-project round. The text follows the repository's plain-writing rules: skills/firstmate/plain-writing.md when that file exists (task T-270 adds it), otherwise the rules quoted in the retro prompt (write for a backend engineer with 3 to 5 years' experience who is new to this repository; explain each term on first use; never use an internal code as the subject of a sentence; keep numbers apart from words; give every item a why and a how). No block, more than one block, invalid JSON, a wrong schema, duplicate ids, a missing locale, more than 20 items, more than 10 generic statements, an 'adds' item without why_not_removal, or items out of the order in 'Removal first' make that round failed and the run failed: answers are kept and no card is raised. Parser tests cover each case.

Reviewed and zero findings. When every round has a valid report, run moves the run to reviewed. If all rounds together have zero items, run completes the run instead, following the completion order in 'After the answer' with an empty answers.json {items:[]}, and appends one wake with identity 'retro-complete-<run-id>' and line 'retro complete: no findings' to the self wake queue only if no line with that identity exists. Tests cover an interrupted and a repeated zero-finding completion (exactly one wake).

Summary card. bin/fm-retro.sh card, for a reviewed run, raises one choice card with the new purpose retro. The card has no owning task, so it takes a hand-raised D-<digits> id. All hand-raised numeric card publication goes through one lock: when bin/lib/fm_retro.py exists next to it, fm-decide.sh publishes a hand-raised numeric id by calling 'python3 bin/lib/fm_retro.py publish-numeric', which, under state/retro/index.lock, checks that no file for that number exists in state/pending/, state/decisions/ or state/runtime/archived-pending/, checks the retro reservation (state/retro/ids/<number>.json holding {run_id}), and only then performs the existing exclusive creation of the pending file. A copied tree without bin/lib/fm_retro.py (several existing test fixtures copy only a list of helpers, for example tests/lib/project-storage.sh) cannot hold retro reservations, so there fm-decide.sh publishes directly exactly as today; tests/board-readiness.test.sh, which publishes a numeric card through such a copy, keeps passing unchanged. card takes the lock, picks the lowest number from 1000 upward with no such file and no reservation, reserves it, writes card.json and the persisted card item order (card-items.json), and releases the lock. It then calls bin/fm-decide.sh --request with purpose retro and --retro-run <run-id>; inside, publish-numeric takes the lock again on its own descriptor, checks again that the reservation still names that run and that no file for the number exists, and publishes. card then takes the lock once more to move the run to awaiting-answer. No process ever waits for a lock it already holds. fm-decide.sh accepts purpose retro only for a hand-raised numeric id without --task whose reservation names that run, and refuses an ordinary hand-raised card on a reserved number. card is idempotent: when card.json exists and that card is pending or answered, it only repairs the run state (see 'After the answer') and raises nothing; when that card was archived, the run becomes failed with reason 'card archived' and no replacement is raised. Tests cover an end-to-end card publication finishing within 30 seconds, a crash between reserving and raising, a repeated card, an ordinary writer that checked before the reservation but publishes after it (refused), and an archived card.

Card content. The card details hold one items list, identical in order and ids in en and zh-TW and identical to card-items.json, 1 to 60 entries, each with id ('<label>/<item-id>', unique), project (the label), title, why, how, evidence and scope. The order is the 'Removal first' grouping across all rounds (removes, then net-removal, then adds); within a group, 'firstmate' items, then self, then external labels in label order, each by item id. Each item on the card shows its effect and what it removes, and an 'adds' item shows its why_not_removal. When the rounds produce more than 60 items, every item stays in the projects' items.json, the first 60 in that order go on the card, and the rest are recorded at once as parked with reason 'card full' and carried to the next retro; the card's notes say how many. External items show their own text, because the card records are a local exception; the card's diagram shows only how many items each label has. bin/lib/fm_ste.py adds items to its field list (bin/lib/fm_ste.py about line 33), checks the text with its existing sentence rules, and checks unique ids and position-by-position equality across locales; fm-decide.sh adds items to the field trigger that runs that check (bin/fm-decide.sh about line 422) and, for purpose retro, checks the ids against card-items.json of the reserved run. items is refused on any card whose purpose is not retro and is never required elsewhere. Tests cover duplicate ids, a substituted item, a reordered translation and an 80-item run.

Retro card options. A retro card offers exactly two options: A (record my choice for each item) and C (park the whole retro). fm-decide.sh's details check, which today requires options A, B and C (bin/fm-decide.sh about line 395), accepts A and C without B only for purpose retro, and refuses B, D or questions on a retro card. Both board card renderers (board/public/index.html, the decision list about line 846 and the card sheet about line 1304) show only A and C and no custom answer for a retro card, and show each item with its own choice of A (approve: firstmate turns it into a task proposal in the item's project), C (park: carried into the next retro) or D (drop). The server refuses chosen B, D or custom on a retro card with 400 'bad choice'. Every other card keeps its current requirements and behaviour.

Answer checks. When the captain answers A on a retro card, POST /decisions requires item_answers: one entry per item, in order, each exactly {index, id, choice}, where index is the zero-based position, id equals that item's id, and choice is A, C or D. Anything else is refused with 400 and code itemAnswersInvalid. When the captain answers C, item_answers must be absent and every item is recorded as parked. The decision record stores item_answers. Answering the same card again must repeat the same chosen and item_answers, as per-question answers already must (board/server.ts about line 2693); a different replay gets 409. Cards without items behave exactly as today. Tests cover acceptance, each refusal, a reordered id, both replays and an unchanged legacy card.

After the answer. Completion is a resumable sequence of four steps: (1) write answers.json, derived from the card's decision record, or {items:[]} for a cardless zero-finding run; (2) set the run's state to completed; (3) advance index.json's last_completed and clear open_run; (4) append the wake, if any. Before performing step k, the run's state.json records completion_step = k (and wake_pending true before step 4); after step 4 it records completion_step = done. Every step is idempotent and done under the index lock, so recovery always redoes the recorded step and continues. record --run accepts only the decision whose id is in card.json and starts or resumes this sequence; a cardless zero-finding completion uses the same sequence with answers {items:[]}. Every entry point, under the lock, first reconciles: it scans state/retro/*/state.json for runs whose completion_step is 1 to 4, and resumes each from the recorded step; it repairs a run still in state reviewed whose card.json names a card that is pending, answered or archived (moving it to awaiting-answer, then on to completion if already answered, or to failed if archived); it marks failed any run in state running whose run.lock is free; it clears open_run when that run is failed. Repeating record with the same answers resumes unfinished steps and otherwise does nothing; a record with different answers or for another card is refused. For every item answered A, firstmate claims, proposes and links it in its own project; nothing is dispatched automatically. Parked items, from per-item C, whole-card C or 'card full', are given to later rounds of the same label with their full id and may be proposed again through carried_from; once a later item that carries one is answered, the earlier entry is marked superseded and is no longer carried. Dropped items are only recorded. Tests restart through an entry point between recording each step and performing it, and after each step, for a card run and for a zero-finding run, and cover a repeated record, a differing record and supersession. Tests also crash card after the card is published but before the run becomes awaiting-answer, then answer the card before recovery, and assert exactly one card and an eventual completion.
